subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Duck Curve Problem
description: A fast breakdown of The Duck Curve Problem for builders.

hook.text: California's grid operators noticed their demand chart looked like a duck. It was a warning.

buildup.text: Midday solar floods the grid with cheap power, pushing demand for other sources down.

discovery.text: At sunset, solar vanishes and demand surges — the grid must ramp up fast to fill the gap.

twist.text: This steep ramp strains power plants not designed to start and stop quickly.

climax.text: Batteries, demand response, and smart pricing are all needed to flatten the duck.

punchline.text: Too much solar at noon is a problem only storage can solve.

quiz.question: What causes the 'duck curve' in electricity demand?
options: Solar floods the grid at midday then vanishes at sunset
People use less power at night

details.summary: The duck curve describes the drop in net electricity demand during midday as solar floods the grid, followed by a steep ramp when solar output falls at sunset and demand peaks. This pattern challenges grid operators, who must rapidly deploy backup power to fill the evening gap.
details.whyItMatters: As solar capacity grows, the duck curve deepens. Managing the sunset ramp is one of the key operational challenges of a high-solar grid and drives investment in storage.
takeaways: Midday solar surplus pushes net demand to very low levels
An extreme ramp occurs at sunset when solar drops off
Battery storage and demand shifting help flatten the curve

faq.question: Where was the duck curve first identified?
faq.answer: The California Independent System Operator coined the term around 2013 after noticing the increasingly duck-shaped net load profile as solar capacity grew. The pattern now appears in sunny regions worldwide with significant solar penetration.

faq.question: How can the duck curve be managed?
faq.answer: Battery storage absorbs midday surplus and discharges at sunset. Time-of-use pricing encourages consumers to shift demand to midday. West-facing panels extend solar generation later. Grid interconnections export surplus to neighboring regions.
